summary: Defines Object Security for Constrained RESTful Environments (OSCORE), which protects CoAP at the application layer using COSE. It gives end-to-end protection between endpoints, even through proxies, and suits constrained devices. It is on the standards track.

eli5.summary: A way for tiny devices to seal their messages in a locked envelope that stays closed even while passing through helpers.

questions: object security for constrained restful environments
how does oscore differ from dtls
how does oscore prevent replay attacks
subtitle: Application-layer encryption for CoAP that stays intact end to end, even when proxies sit in the middle.

tldr.problem: CoAP is normally secured with DTLS or TLS, which end at every proxy, so a proxy can read, change, drop or reorder the messages it forwards.
tldr.mechanism: OSCORE wraps the sensitive parts of a CoAP request or response in a compressed COSE object protected with an AEAD algorithm, and leaves only the fields a proxy needs in the clear.
tldr.outcome: Client and server get end-to-end encryption, integrity, replay protection and binding of each response to its request, with a small per-message overhead. It is a Proposed Standard that updates RFC 7252.

today: RFC 8613 is a Proposed Standard published in July 2019. It updates RFC 7252 and has not been obsoleted.

sections.title: Why CoAP Needs Object Security
sections.content:
The Constrained Application Protocol (CoAP, RFC 7252) is a web transfer protocol for constrained nodes and networks. It relies on proxies for scalability and on DTLS for security. The catch is that CoAP-to-CoAP, HTTP-to-CoAP and CoAP-to-HTTP proxies require (D)TLS to be terminated at the proxy. The proxy can then eavesdrop on, or manipulate, any part of the payload and metadata, and can inject, delete or reorder packets.

OSCORE (Object Security for Constrained RESTful Environments) protects CoAP and CoAP-mappable HTTP requests and responses end to end, across forward proxies and cross-protocol translators. It builds on COSE (RFC 8152) and uses pre-shared keys that were set up out of band or by a key establishment protocol. It supports the Observe, Block-wise and No-Response options and the PATCH and FETCH methods.

OSCORE protects the RESTful interaction (method, resource, payload and so on). It does not protect the CoAP messaging layer or the Token. The application decides when OSCORE is required, and it can be combined with (D)TLS on some or all hops.
sections.eli5: Normal secure mail gets opened and re-sealed at every post office. OSCORE seals the letter once, at the sender, and only the final reader opens it.

sections.title: The Security Context
sections.content:
Client and server must share a security context. Each endpoint's context has three parts. The Common Context holds the AEAD algorithm, the HKDF algorithm, the Master Secret, an optional Master Salt, an optional ID Context and the Common IV. The Sender Context holds the Sender ID, the Sender Key and the Sender Sequence Number. The Recipient Context holds the Recipient ID, the Recipient Key and, on servers, a Replay Window.

An endpoint protects what it sends with its Sender Context and verifies what it receives with its Recipient Context. One side's Sender ID is the other side's Recipient ID, so the two contexts are partly mirrored.

Only the Master Secret, Sender ID and Recipient ID must be preestablished. Defaults cover the rest: AES-CCM-16-64-128 (COSE algorithm encoding 10), an empty Master Salt, HKDF SHA-256, and an anti-replay sliding window of size 32. The Sender Key, Recipient Key and Common IV are derived from these inputs with HKDF, using a CBOR array info made of the id, the ID Context, the AEAD algorithm, a type string (Key or IV) and the length L.

To keep keys unique, the pair (ID Context, Sender ID) MUST be unique among all contexts that share a Master Secret and Master Salt. The maximum Sender ID length is the AEAD nonce length minus 6 bytes, which is 7 bytes for AES-CCM-16-64-128.
sections.eli5: Two friends agree on a secret codebook beforehand. Each keeps one page for writing and a matching page for reading, so what one writes the other can read.

sections.title: What Is Protected and What Is Not
sections.content:
OSCORE sorts every message field into a class. Class E fields are encrypted and integrity protected. Class I fields are integrity protected only, and Class U fields are left unprotected. The RFC notes that no Class I options are currently defined. Class E fields travel inside the ciphertext (called Inner). Class U fields stay in the header or options, visible to proxies (called Outer).

The CoAP Code and the payload are Class E. The real Code is moved into the encrypted plaintext, and the outer Code is set to 0.02 (POST) for requests and 2.04 (Changed) for responses, so an intermediary cannot see or change a GET into a DELETE. The Version, Type, Length, Token Length, Message ID and Token fields are Class U, because proxies need them.

Among options, Uri-Path, Uri-Query, ETag, Content-Format and Location-Path are Inner only. Uri-Host, Uri-Port, Proxy-Uri and Proxy-Scheme are Outer only, so forward proxies still work. Observe, Max-Age, the Block options, Size1, Size2 and No-Response can have both an Inner and an Outer instance. Unknown options are treated as Class E.

Outer Block options are neither encrypted nor integrity protected, so a proxy could keep injecting fragments. Applications MUST therefore set a maximum unfragmented message size and discard messages that exceed it.
sections.eli5: Think of a parcel: the contents are locked inside, but the shipping label has to stay readable so the carriers know where to send it.

sections.title: The COSE Object, Nonce and AAD
sections.content:
OSCORE uses an untagged COSE_Encrypt0 object with an AEAD algorithm. AES-CCM-16-64-128 is mandatory to implement. For it the keys are 128 bits and the nonce and Common IV are 13 bytes. The 'protected' field is empty. The 'unprotected' field carries the Partial IV (the Sender Sequence Number with leading zero bytes removed), the kid (the Sender ID) and optionally a kid context (the ID Context). Partial IV and kid are always present in requests and typically absent from responses.

The plaintext is the original Code, the Inner options, and the payload prefixed by the payload marker 0xff if there is one. The AAD includes an external_aad array with the OSCORE version (which MUST be 1), the algorithms, the request's kid and Partial IV, and any Class I options.

The nonce is built by padding the Partial IV to 5 bytes, padding the Sender ID of the endpoint that generated the Partial IV to nonce length minus 6 bytes, prefixing a single byte holding that ID's size, and XORing the result with the Common IV. If a response carries no Partial IV, the request's nonce is reused.
sections.eli5: Each message gets its own one-time lock setting, made from a counter and the sender's name, so no two messages ever use the same setting.

sections.title: Header Compression
sections.content:
COSE is built for stateless use and adds more overhead than a stateful protocol needs. OSCORE therefore defines a stateless compression that removes redundant information. The result is the compressed COSE object, split across two CoAP fields: the OSCORE option carries the headers and the payload carries the ciphertext.

The OSCORE option value starts with a flag byte. The three least significant bits give the Partial IV length n (values 6 and 7 are reserved), the next bit is the kid flag k, and the one after is the kid context flag h. The remaining three bits are reserved and must be zero, otherwise the message is malformed. After the flag byte come the Partial IV, then a length byte and the kid context if h is set, and finally the kid, which MUST be the last field.

The RFC's first example is a request with kid 0x25 and Partial IV 0x05. Compression shrinks it from 24 bytes to 17, with option value 0x090525 and a 14-byte payload. If all flag bits are zero, the option value is empty.
sections.eli5: Instead of writing a long letter heading every time, you use a short code that both sides already understand. The message gets much shorter.

sections.title: Processing, Freshness and Replay Protection
sections.content:
To protect a request, the client gets the Sender Context, builds the AAD and plaintext, encodes the Partial IV and increments the Sender Sequence Number, computes the nonce, encrypts and compresses the COSE object, and formats the OSCORE message with the OSCORE option. The server discards the outer Code and Class E options, decompresses the object, finds the Recipient Context from the kid (and kid context), checks the Replay Window, rebuilds the AAD and nonce, and decrypts. If decryption fails, the server stops processing and MAY answer 4.00 (Bad Request).

An AEAD nonce MUST NOT be used more than once per key. The Sender Sequence Number must be less than 2^40, and past the maximum the endpoint MUST NOT process more messages with that context. Reading and increasing the number, and checking and updating the replay window, MUST each be atomic.

Responses are bound to requests: the request's kid and Partial IV go into the response's AAD, so a response cannot be matched to a different request. For requests OSCORE only guarantees they are not older than the security context, so applications needing stronger freshness must add a mechanism such as the Echo option.

If a device loses its Sender Sequence Number or Replay Window, for example on an unplanned reboot, it must recover safely. The RFC lists options including careful use of nonvolatile memory, deriving new contexts from the Master Secret, a trusted third party, or a key exchange. A key exchange is necessary when forward secrecy is required.
sections.eli5: Every message has a numbered ticket, and the receiver crosses off tickets it has seen. If someone tries to reuse an old ticket, it is turned away.

sections.title: Proxies and HTTP
sections.content:
OSCORE is designed to work with OSCORE-unaware CoAP forward proxies. An OSCORE-aware proxy can do better: it SHALL bypass caching for requests with the OSCORE option and SHOULD avoid caching their responses. It SHALL NOT start an Observe registration. Error responses may carry an Outer Max-Age of zero to stop pointless caching.

For HTTP, the OSCORE option value is carried in a new OSCORE HTTP header field as base64url without padding (an empty option becomes AA), and the HTTP Content-Type is application/oscore. The field is used only in POST requests and in responses with status 200. This lets OSCORE run end to end between, for example, an HTTP client and a CoAP server through a cross-protocol proxy. Because the HTTP body must survive redirects, servers are RECOMMENDED to use 307 or 308 rather than 301 or 302.

A resource reachable only through OSCORE can be flagged with the osc attribute in a web link. It is only a hint and carries no key material.
sections.eli5: The post office can move the locked box between different delivery services, such as a van or a plane, without ever being able to open it.

sections.title: Security and Privacy Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC argues that hop-by-hop protection forces trust in every intermediary, which is problematic even when the owners are fully trusted, since intermediaries could delete resources on sensors or falsify commands to actuators. OSCORE protects end to end everything not needed for proxy operations. It can be combined with (D)TLS, and when OSCORE is used with HTTP, additional TLS on the HTTP hops is RECOMMENDED.

The Master Secret must be secret and have a good amount of randomness. Sharing a security context between servers can open the door to replay attacks if the Replay Windows are not synchronized, and an attacker may try to force a reboot to replay a message. A verified request shows who made it but not that the client is still alive, for which the server may use the Echo option.

On privacy, unprotected fields still leak information: the Token, Message ID and Type allow traffic analysis and request matching, 'kid' and 'kid context' can let an observer correlate one client's requests, and unprotected errors reveal security state. Message lengths can leak information, and applications may use padding.
sections.eli5: The locked box hides what is inside, but people can still see the box's size and who keeps sending boxes. So some small clues can leak, even though the contents stay secret.
